entry.title: India's carbon credit market needs liquidity and credible price signals
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / India's carbon credit market needs liquidity and credible price signalsIndia's carbon credit market needs liquidity and credible price signals

The need is to have liquidity and depth in the market

premium

Illustration: Ajaya Kumar Mohanty

Ajay TyagiDiya Shah6 min read Last Updated : Nov 15 2026 | 10:34 PM ISTIt is good news that the United Kingdom has recognised India’s Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (CCTS) as a pricing mechanism under its Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), which takes effect in January next year. The benefit to Indian exporters, however, rests entirely on the carbon price the CCTS produces.  The CCTS, as it exists today, needs much improvement. This column focuses on how to have liquidity and depth in the carbon-trading market so that the scheme throws up the right and credible carbon price.  To begin with, the scheme should ensure that there is sufficient demand for carbon-credit certificates (CCCs) in the market at any given time. All the proposed units in different sectors, as announced under the scheme, should be notified in one go. Apart from building demand, this will improve liquidity in the market. The exclusion of high-emitting sectors such as thermal power, which accounts for roughly 40 per cent of national emission, makes no sense. Further, at present, the scheme sets different targets for greenhouse-gas emission for different units in a sector, based on their past emission levels; the laggards in the past have been given softer targets. This is sure to kill demand, besides being unfair to better-performing units. All this would result in an illiquid market and a weak price, not reflective of the true price. The similar category of units within a sector, based on a criterion like revenue or asset size, should be given the same targets. For instance, the integrated steel plants  of similar production capacity should be given the same targets.More importantly, the targets ought to be ambitious from the very beginning, in line with our emission reduction commitments,  and the MRV (measurement, reporting and verification) framework robust. Going forward, more sectors should be notified under the scheme at the earliest.  Under the scheme, entities performing better than the targets would be entitled to get CCCs, which would be credited in their accounts, free of cost, by the Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE). Underperforming entities can then purchase the required CCCs in the market from those having them.  On the trading of CCCs, one could perhaps take a leaf out of the highly successful process followed in the stock market, though admittedly CCCs and stocks are different.  Like stock exchanges (SEs), the exchanges on which CCCs would trade (herein after referred to as exchanges) may keep a small window before the start of trading day for call auction to determine the opening price of a CCC. In case there is no participation by entities in the call auction, the previous-day closing price will be the opening price. The closing price will be the volume-adjusted weighted average price (VWAP) derived during the last half an hour of trading in the day. Depending on the level of volatility in trading prices at any given time, the exchanges may prescribe a price band, with the floor and ceiling being a certain percentage of the price. The clearing and settlement mechanism may be through a clearing corporation. There are two suggestions for improving liquidity in the carbon-trading market. The exchanges may introduce a market-making scheme in the first few years of trading. Market makers are financial institutions that simultaneously give “buy” and “sell” quotes to improve liquidity. Of course, they would need to be compensated for the losses incurred by them. SEs have schemes on market making for illiquid stocks, eg stocks for small and medium enterprises. The exchanges could learn from the experience of SEs.  The other suggestion to improve the depth of the market is to introduce derivatives trading for CCCs. The obligated entities could lock in compliance costs by buying futures. Futures prices would give an early signal of where the carbon price is heading. The European Union’s Emissions Trading System (EU-ETS) shows the scale this can reach. Nearly 90 per cent of allowances trade as futures, and about 65 per cent of secondary-market participants are financial players who typically sell the futures that compliance firms buy to protect themselves against rising prices. South Korea offers what happens in the absence of financial players. With financial participants initially excluded, allowance trading stalled for eight months in 2015, and only 0.06 per cent of allocated allowances changed hands in the first year. After state banks were appointed market makers in 2019 and financial intermediaries were admitted, annual traded volumes rose from 5.66 million tonnes in 2015 to 54.72 million tonnes by 2021.  While the market for CCCs may be regulated by the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (CERC), the futures market may come under the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) like it does for the derivatives market for commodities. A similar arrangement exists for electricity trading. Electricity futures, launched in July 2025, rest on a clear division of roles. The CERC oversees physical power trading on the exchanges, while Sebi regulates futures settled in cash against those exchange prices. A clearing corporation guarantees every contract and collects margins upfront, and protect against defaults. Within their first year, futures volumes on the National Stock Exchange alone reached roughly half the physical day-ahead market, evidence that hedging demand exists once the infrastructure is in place.  The futures on CCCs should trade on  Sebi-regulated exchanges, and settled against the VWAP prices discovered in the physical market. The overall and participant-specific position limits, as a percentage of the trading volumes in the physical market, would need to be put to ensure that the futures market doesn’t manipulate the physical market.  The CCTS begins on a rather tentative note. The scheme was notified in 2023 but trading is yet to start. It is not a good idea to begin the scheme on a weak footing. Any failure would be seen as a non-serious attempt by the government. Except for the suggestions relating to the derivatives market, all other suggestions made above, including allowing financial institutions participation as market makers, may be made part of the scheme right away. The derivatives market may be introduced later at an appropriate time, but the intention to develop it in future should find mention in the scheme now itself so as to give the right message to the world at large about our commitment to develop a credible carbon market in the country. 
The writers are, respectively, former chairman, Sebi, and research assistant, Observer Research Foundation   Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: Short covering and foreign inflows are fuelling Indian stock market rebound
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Short covering and foreign inflows are fuelling Indian stock market reboundShort covering and foreign inflows are fuelling Indian stock market rebound

In the three weeks to November 13, the Nifty 50 surged 11.3 per cent, from 22,600 to 25,144, with almost all the gains concentrated in a single spectacular week

premium

Investors who had sold futures had to buy them back, adding demand just as cash-market buying gathered pace (Representative Image)

Debashis Basu5 min read Last Updated : Nov 15 2026 | 11:49 PM ISTFor much of 2025 and 2026, India’s stock market had an awkward problem: The economy was growing, corporate earnings were improving, yet foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) were heading for the exits. Earlier, India was the emerging market that global investors worried about not owning. For two years, it was the one they could do without. In Bank of America’s Asia Fund Manager Survey, India was the least preferred Asian stock market, with the absence of a clear artificial-intelligence (AI) opportunity as the biggest concern, followed by weak growth, high valuations, and insufficient reform. Newspaper editorials were amplifying the alarm, asking policymakers to heed the warning. The pessimism was overdone. As I mentioned in August this year, the underlying reality was far from alarming. In late October, the tide turned dramatically.  In the three weeks to November 13, the Nifty 50 surged 11.3 per cent, from 22,600 to 25,144, with almost all the gains concentrated in a single spectacular week. Between October 30 and November 6, the benchmark rose 8.6 per cent, its strongest weekly performance in roughly six years. Five forces converged. One, the government hinted that it would consider removing the main irritant for FPIs — long-term capital gains tax. Two, the unwinding of the crowded AI trade in other Asian markets encouraged FPIs to diversify towards India. Three, a sharp fall in prices of crude oil improved India’s external economic prospects. Four, by late October, FPIs had built huge bearish positions in index futures. The rally triggered by FPI buying was turbocharged by powerful short-covering. Five, better corporate earnings provided fundamental support. After months of selling, overseas investors bought Indian equities worth $6.43 billion up to November 12, their biggest monthly purchase in more than two years.  Of the five reasons, the global retreat from the AI trade is the most amusing. In my piece in August, I had argued that the biggest reason to ignore the FPI griping was that India’s listed stocks had little exposure to the current AI mania. That gripe ignored the fact that only Taiwan and South Korea, among countries outside the United States and China, could offer significant exposure to the AI fashion. I had said that no policymaker should lose sleep over this. It would be akin to shunning a country in 1999 because it did not have loss-making listed internet companies, or in 2007 because it did not have financial stocks minting money from toxic subprime mortgages. From the second week of October, American AI stocks, semiconductor makers in Taiwan and South Korea, and suppliers of data-centre infrastructure began a deep dive as investors started to question whether these represented an expensive wager on returns that had yet to materialise. In October, foreigners withdrew nearly $50 billion from seven Asian equity markets, much of it from Taiwan and South Korea. India, with little exposure to the semiconductor supply chain, became a destination for investors seeking diversification.  Meanwhile, Brent crude, which approached $113 a barrel on October 30, fell by about a fifth from its peak before trading near $92 on November 12. The decline reflected reduced fears of further escalation in the Iran conflict and hopes of de-escalation after America’s midterm elections. For India, which imports close to 90 per cent of its oil, the benefits are immediate: A smaller import bill, less pressure on the current account and the rupee, and lower imported inflation. The rupee strengthened by about 1.1 per cent in the week to November 6, its best weekly performance since April. A firm currency makes Indian assets less risky for dollar-based investors, creates a virtuous circle of lower oil prices, a steadier rupee, and renewed inflows. The markets were pricing in a greater chance of deescalation, not settled peace.  The speed of the advance owed much to the unusually large bearish FPI position in Nifty futures, with net shorts estimated at around 280,000 contracts near October 23. Once the index rose, those bets became costly. Investors who had sold futures had to buy them back, adding demand just as cash-market buying gathered pace. By November 6, net shorts had fallen to about 100,000 contracts and Nifty futures open interest had dropped by roughly 22 per cent. Foreign investors were also net buyers of about ₹27,600 crore of index futures over seven trading sessions to November 12. This was a classic short-covering episode, further amplified by substantial actual purchases of shares in the cash market. Of the 50 Nifty companies reporting results, 27 beat analyst estimates. Sales and operating profits rose 22 per cent. Foreign buying is usually concentrated in large, liquid companies, particularly financial stocks, whose weighting in the Nifty gives each rupee of demand an outsize influence. In the first week of November, Shriram Finance rose 16.8 per cent, Bajaj Finance 15.8 per cent, Mahindra & Mahindra 15.7 per cent, HDFC Bank 13.8 per cent, and Reliance Industries 13.3 per cent.  What comes next? A powerful rally after a long period of listlessness can set the stage for a prolonged rise, the reasons for which are sometimes unfathomable. From a deeply pessimistic market in late December 2011, the Nifty staged a remarkable seven-week rally of 21 per cent up to the third week of February 2012, with no clear explanation. It is quite another matter that over the next three months almost all the gains had been wiped out. There is no way to tell whether this is the beginning of another long bull market, particularly if the stalemate in the Strait of Hormuz remains unresolved. However, I remain bullish on smaller Indian companies and the domestic fund flows that support them. This is a durable trend which I have highlighted several times this year.

entry.title: Clean books, thin margins: The new reality of Indian banking
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Clean books, thin margins: The new reality of Indian bankingClean books, thin margins: The new reality of Indian banking

As the rate cycle turns, margins should get some relief, but how banks navigate emerging stress in unsecured personal and gold loans remains to be seen

premium

Representative Image

Tamal Bandyopadhyay7 min read Last Updated : Nov 15 2026 | 10:53 PM ISTWalk into the treasury floor of any bank today, and you’re certain to hear a sigh of relief among dealers. After nearly touching 7.5 per cent in late October, the 10-year benchmark government bond yield is now consolidating between 7.1 per cent and 7.2 per cent.  Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions: When yields rise, bond values fall, triggering a mark-to-market (MTM) hit on banks' treasury income. The country's largest lender, State Bank of India (SBI), saw its treasury income drop about 20 per cent year-on-year (y-o-y) in the September quarter, weighed down by both the earlier uptick in bond yields and a depreciating rupee.  A recent report by CareEdge Ratings pegs the fall in treasury income across select scheduled commercial banks in the September quarter at 61.6 per cent y-o-y. Private sector banks saw a 65.7 per cent drop, sharper than their public sector peers at 59.4 per cent. As bond yields hardened towards the end of the quarter, banks were forced to book MTM losses—the notional loss recognised when the market value of securities falls below their book value, even if they are not sold—and had fewer opportunities to book trading profits.  Another pain point is the persistent squeeze in low-cost current account and savings account (Casa) deposits. All listed universal banks reported a y-o-y drop in their Casa ratio, barring five. Three of them are in the public sector (Indian Overseas Bank or IOB, Union Bank of India and Indian Bank) and two in the private sector (Federal Bank Ltd and Karnataka Bank Ltd). For a few, the contraction was 4 percentage points or more. Among the five exceptions, only IOB recorded a rise—albeit marginal—on both a y-o-y and quarter-on-quarter (q-o-q) basis.  IDFC FIRST Bank Ltd leads the industry with a Casa ratio of 48.4 per cent, followed by Bank of Maharashtra (46.47 per cent), Central Bank of India (44.65 per cent), IDBI Bank Ltd (43.82 per cent), Jammu & Kashmir Bank Ltd (41.97 per cent) and IOB (40.71 per cent). No other bank has crossed the 40 per cent mark. Among large lenders, SBI, ICICI Bank Ltd and Kotak Mahindra Bank Ltd maintained a Casa ratio of at least 38 per cent each, while Axis Bank Ltd had 36 per cent and HDFC Bank Ltd 31.6 per cent. For some lenders, large inflows of foreign currency non-resident (FCNR-B) deposits swelled the term deposit base and pulled the ratio down.  Another headache for bankers is the continued compression in net interest margin (NIM)—broadly, the spread between a bank's yield on advances and its cost of funds. Large private sector lenders bore the brunt of this squeeze due to elevated deposit costs, intense competition for retail funds, and the thin margins earned on the FCNR-B deposits mobilised in large volumes during the quarter.  HDFC Bank's NIM fell 11 basis points (bps) y-o-y and 10 bps q-o-q to 3.16 per cent in the September quarter, its lowest on record. ICICI Bank's margin dropped 12 bps y-o-y and 18 bps sequentially to 4.18 per cent. Axis Bank saw a sharper contraction—down 37 bps y-o-y and 10 bps q-o-q to 3.36 per cent. SBI bucked the trend: Its domestic NIM rose 11 bps sequentially to 3.11 per cent. At 2.94 per cent, its whole-bank NIM was down 3 bps y-o-y but up 8 bps q-o-q. One bps is a hundredth of a percentage point.  Subdued treasury income is a cyclical phenomenon—it routinely occurs when yields harden. The persistent erosion in Casa and NIM, however, points to deeper structural shifts. A steady slide in Casa reflects a fundamental change in how Indian savers deploy their money, forcing banks to adapt to higher funding costs as competition intensifies.  Yet one metric on bank balance sheets signals a far more profound structural transformation and underscores how the business of banking is evolving. No prizes for guessing: It is the steady, continuous decline in bad assets.  Just one public sector bank (PSB) currently has a net non-performing asset (NPA) ratio above 0.5 per cent, alongside five private sector lenders. These six banks are Bandhan Bank Ltd (92 bps), IndusInd Bank Ltd (83 bps), Karnataka Bank Ltd (74 bps), DCB Bank Ltd (73 bps), Punjab & Sind Bank (61 bps) and Jammu & Kashmir Bank (51 bps).  What’s more, every listed bank reported a y-o-y drop in net NPAs in the September quarter. All but one—IDBI Bank—recorded a reduction both y-o-y and q-o-q. IDBI Bank reported a net NPA ratio of 17 bps, down from 21 bps a year ago, though marginally higher than 16 bps in the June quarter.  Among the mega-lenders, SBI reported a net NPA ratio of 36 bps, HDFC Bank 37 bps, ICICI Bank 30 bps and Axis Bank 35 bps. South Indian Bank Ltd boasted the lowest net NPA ratio in the industry at 9 bps, followed by Bank of Maharashtra (12 bps), Tamilnad Mercantile Bank Ltd and Indian Bank (14 bps each), and IOB (16 bps).  On gross NPAs, only two lenders kept their ratio below 1 per cent—Tamilnad Mercantile Bank (61 bps) and Karur Vysya Bank Ltd (69 bps). Next came RBL Bank Ltd (102 bps), Kotak Mahindra Bank (104 bps), HDFC Bank (111 bps), Axis Bank (116 bps), IOB (119 bps), and ICICI Bank and Yes Bank Ltd (120 bps each). SBI's gross NPA ratio stood at 139 bps, its lowest in more than two decades.  In absolute terms, PSBs' gross NPAs fell 12.9 per cent y-o-y to Rs 2.31 trillion at the end of September, while private banks saw a 6.7 per cent drop to Rs 1.28 trillion. Across all listed banks, gross NPAs contracted by 10.8 per cent.  On the net NPA front, PSBs recorded a 13.3 per cent drop to Rs 44,092 crore, while private banks logged a 7.7 per cent decline to Rs 34,606 crore. Aggregate net NPAs across all listed banks fell 10.9 per cent.  To put this turnaround in perspective, gross NPAs of all scheduled commercial banks in India (including foreign banks and small finance banks) had peaked at Rs 10.36 trillion in the fourth quarter of FY18, with net NPAs at Rs 5.21 trillion. At that peak, PSBs accounted for Rs 8.96 trillion of gross NPAs—a staggering 14.6 per cent ratio—and Rs 4.54 trillion of net NPAs (8 per cent). Private banks' gross NPAs then stood at Rs 1.29 trillion (4.7 per cent) and net NPAs at Rs 64,380 crore (2.4 per cent).  On most operational metrics today, PSBs are outperforming their private sector peers. Their operating profits grew 17.2 per cent y-o-y in the September quarter, compared with 13.5 per cent for private banks. Total operating profit for all listed banks rose 15.4 per cent to Rs 1.81 trillion. SBI led with Rs 34,226 crore in operating profit, followed by HDFC Bank (Rs 29,483 crore), ICICI Bank (Rs 20,576 crore), Bank of Baroda (Rs 11,430 crore) and Axis Bank (Rs 11,083 crore). No other lender crossed the Rs 10,000 crore mark.  After setting aside Rs 27,271 crore in provisions for bad loans (down 9.1 per cent y-o-y, though up 7.2 per cent sequentially), aggregate net profit for all listed banks rose 20.1 per cent y-o-y to Rs 1.16 trillion. PSBs and private banks ran neck-and-neck in profit growth. Three lenders crossed the Rs 10,000 crore net profit mark: SBI (Rs 23,038 crore), HDFC Bank (Rs 19,510 crore) and ICICI Bank (Rs 14,843 crore).  So far, the run has been remarkable. In a rising interest rate cycle, floating rate loans reprice upward faster than deposits, lifting NIMs. That should ease the margin squeeze in the coming quarters. But how banks navigate the emerging stress in unsecured personal loans and gold-collateralised lending, however, remains to be seen. ____________________________________________________________________________________________________ The writer is an author and senior advisor to Jana Small Finance Bank Ltd. entry.title: Consumer Protection: Insured should not sign away right to full claim
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Consumer Protection: Insured should not sign away right to full claimConsumer Protection: Insured should not sign away right to full claim

The National Commission has held that insistence on a full and final discharge is not justified, as it deprives the insured of their right to take legal action for the balance claim

premium

Policyholders should not sign full and final discharge vouchers if they intend to pursue the balance of their insurance claims.

Jehangir B Gai3 min read Last Updated : Nov 15 2026 | 10:18 PM ISTLosses suffered by a business can have devastating consequences, not only for the insured but also for its employees and others connected with it. If a business ceases to function, its employees lose their livelihood, while creditors find it challenging to recover the value of goods supplied on credit. Meanwhile, interest and other fixed expenses keep rising, resulting in a crushing financial burden on the insured.  The very purpose of insurance is to insulate a business and safeguard it against unexpected losses. This can happen only if the insurer promptly assesses and settles the claim. Unfortunately, the sad reality is that insurers generally keep claims pending for months. Even when the insurer assesses a claim, it makes several deductions that may or may not be acceptable to the insured.  In cases where the insurer does not pay the full claim, it invariably insists on a full and final discharge before releasing the amount offered. The insured, meanwhile, wants to accept the settlement conditionally, without prejudice to his right to claim the remaining amount that the insurer has disallowed. However, insurers usually capitalise on the insured’s financial predicament and refuse to release the assessed amount, so that they obtain a full and final discharge and the insured forfeits his right to claim the balance. In this column, I will deal with the rights of an insured who finds himself in such a situation.  What does the law say?   The law is well settled that once the insured executes a full and final discharge voucher, he would ordinarily not have the right to claim the balance amount, as the Supreme Court of India held in New India Assurance Co v Genus Power Infrastructure.  An exception to this general rule is permissible only if the insured can establish that he executed the discharge voucher due to coercion, as the Supreme Court of India  laid down in United India Insurance v Ajmer Singh Cotton & General Mills & Ors. Here, the court emphasised that executing discharge vouchers does not inherently prevent policyholders from seeking additional compensation if they can demonstrate that the insurer obtained the vouchers through fraudulent means or undue influence. However, the burden of proof is on the insured, and it is not easy to establish coercion.  The viable remedy  The National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (NCDRC) has held that such insistence on a full and final discharge is not justified, as it deprives the insured of their right to take legal action for the balance claim. It held that when the insured gives a discharge “under protest”, the insurer must pay the admitted amount, and withholding it would constitute an unfair trade practice. Hence, in K L Malhotra v Oriental Insurance Co Ltd & Anr and Abhay Neelawarne v New India Assurance Co Ltd & Anr, it issued general directions to stop such unfair practices and ordered the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (Irdai) to issue appropriate instructions.  What should the insured do?  An insured must refuse to execute a full and final discharge if he wants to take legal action to recover the balance claim amount. The remedy lies in filing a consumer complaint and applying for interim relief directing the insurer to release the admitted amount.  The writer is a consumer activist     Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: The business case for women entrepreneurs: Unlocking credit potential
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / The business case for women entrepreneurs: Unlocking credit potentialThe business case for women entrepreneurs: Unlocking credit potential

Women borrowers are emerging as a key growth driver for lenders, offering higher credit growth, lower delinquencies and significant untapped business potential

premium

India’s next phase of credit growth hinges on how effectively lenders serve women entrepreneurs by designing products for them

Manish Shah4 min read Last Updated : Nov 15 2026 | 9:24 PM ISTFor decades, access to formal credit has been a powerful engine of economic mobility. In India, one of the most significant developments in the credit ecosystem is the growing presence of women borrowers. What began as a financial inclusion effort has steadily evolved into a compelling economic opportunity for financial institutions.  Women borrowers have over the past five years grown at a compound annual growth rate of 14.2 per cent (compared to 8.2 per cent for men), reaching 89 million by December 2025 and accounting for nearly 28 per cent of the retail credit base, according to CRIF High Mark's March 2026 report called The Credit Goes to Her. Their credit portfolios are expanding faster, with 23.4 per cent year-on-year growth (16.7 per cent for men), while active loans are growing more than twice as fast. This positions women as key drivers of incremental credit demand. Women exhibit lower delinquency rates at 2.8 per cent (3.3 per cent for men). Their role in productive credit is also rising steadily, with secured business loans to women growing over 61 per cent year-on-year and accounting for more than half of loan volumes. Women are also the fastest-growing segment of first-time borrowers, with their share in new-to-credit originations increasing from 33 per cent to 41 per cent in two years.  These trends make a compelling case: Women borrowers offer higher growth, lower risk and long-term value, making them central to the future of lending. The rise of the woman entrepreneur is seen from neighbourhood retail outlets and service businesses to emerging digital ventures. Across sectors and geographies, more women are moving beyond participation and becoming key economic contributors and business decision-makers. This shift is particularly visible in smaller cities and emerging markets, where access to formal finance is enabling women entrepreneurs to scale businesses, generate employment and contribute meaningfully to local economies.  Despite encouraging progress, several structural challenges continue to shape women’s access to credit. Collateral ownership remains limited, with many women lacking formal property titles required for secured lending. Financial awareness and confidence gaps also continue to influence borrowing behaviour, particularly in smaller markets. In addition, digital access gaps persist across certain borrower segments, even as digital lending platforms expand rapidly.  Encouragingly, government initiatives have helped address some of these barriers. Programmes such as the Pradhan Mantri Mudra Yojana have enabled millions of women to access formal credit. Institutional support has also strengthened women-led self-help group networks, helping connect rural borrowers to the formal banking system. These developments reinforce an important principle: When women gain access to formal finance, they use it productively and repay it responsibly.  A critical gap persists between social-sector lending and mainstream commercial finance for women. While microfinance and self-help groups have enabled access to small-ticket credit, many women entrepreneurs struggle to transition into larger, formal lending ecosystems. This creates a “missing middle”, where businesses are too large for microfinance yet not adequately served by traditional banking. As a result, women-led enterprises continue to face a significant financing gap, estimated to be as high as 70 per cent, representing a large untapped opportunity for formal financial institutions.  Bridging this gap will require a shift in how lenders assess and serve women borrowers. Despite demonstrating strong repayment behaviour, women often receive smaller loan sizes and limited access to growth capital. Addressing this calls for more inclusive underwriting models, greater use of alternative data and stronger support systems.  For lenders, the path forward is clear. Women borrowers represent a high-quality credit segment that remains underserved relative to its potential. Financial institutions that invest early in this segment will not only support economic inclusion but also strengthen their own business fundamentals. Designing products tailored for women entrepreneurs, building advisory support mechanisms and expanding outreach can unlock long-term value.  In many ways, the next phase of credit growth will be shaped by how effectively the financial ecosystem engages with women entrepreneurs.
  The writer is the managing director and chief executive officer of Godrej Capital     Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: Scotch at the docks tests India-UK trade arrangement's tariff concessions
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Scotch at the docks tests India-UK trade arrangement's tariff concessionsScotch at the docks tests India-UK trade arrangement's tariff concessions

The India-UK trade pact offers lower duties on eligible Scotch whisky imports, but the applicable tariff depends on the classification of goods under the Customs Tariff and exemption notification

premium

The India-UK trade agreement envisages an initial duty of 75 per cent on imports of eligible Scotch whisky, with the rate falling to 40 per cent over 10 years

TNC Rajagopalan3 min read Last Updated : Nov 15 2026 | 6:18 PM ISTLast week, Reuters reported that several consignments of Scotch whisky imported from the United Kingdom (UK) were held up at the ports. The importers seek clearance at 75 per cent Customs duty under the India-UK trade agreement, whereas the Customs seek duty at 150 per cent. On Friday, the Commerce Secretary said that the Ministry of Finance had engaged with the stakeholders and that India would honour the duty concessions under the agreement.  The India-UK trade agreement envisages an initial duty of 75 per cent on imports of eligible Scotch whisky, with the rate falling to 40 per cent over 10 years. Entries at serial numbers 827 and 830 of Table I to notification No. 29/2026-Cus dated July 14, 2026, give effect to the initial concession. Both entries say “All goods” against tariff items 22083012 and 22083092 and prescribe 25 per cent basic Customs duty (BCD) and 50 per cent Agriculture Infrastructure and Development Cess (AIDC), subject to the conditions in the notification, including those relating to origin.  The case of the Directorate of Revenue Intelligence (DRI) appears to be that the items imported are concentrates or compound alcoholic preparations of a kind used for the manufacture of beverages. According to Reuters, the DRI, in a memo dated November 4, asked the Customs field formations  to apply the higher rate to such goods. The investigators reportedly take the view that the concession applies to finished products such as bottled Scotch. The distinction to be made is between whisky as imported and an alcoholic preparation used to make a beverage. UK verification guidance recognises that Scotch whisky can be shipped in bulk at high strength and diluted before bottling.  In October, India and the UK cited Scotch whisky as an early success of their trade agreement. Their October 12 joint statement said it had already entered India at reduced tariffs, without giving particulars of the goods cleared. Incidentally, tariff item 21069051 entered the Customs Tariff on May 1, 2026, through the Finance Act, 2026, when tariff item 21069050 was split into 21069051 and 21069059. The new item for compound alcoholic preparations carries 150 per cent BCD. The July notification gives no concession against that entry.  Interestingly, the DGFT’s ITC (HS) import schedule gives the description against 22083092 as Scotch in containers holding more than two litres. The Customs Tariff gives the description “Scotch” against both 22083012 and 22083092 under the six-digit subheading 220830 for whiskies. The first item comes under “In containers holding 2 litres or less” and the second under “Other”. The word "Other" must be read at the same level as the preceding description relating to container size.  So, Scotch whisky in containers holding more than two litres gets the same concession as Scotch whisky in smaller containers. If, however, the goods as imported answer to the description of compound alcoholic preparations under tariff item 21069051, Customs would be on firmer ground in denying the exemption.  Importers should, therefore, go by the actual wording of the exemption notification issued by the Ministry of Finance, read with the Customs tariff. The text of the trade agreement, government press releases and reports in the media may help them understand the concession but importers should satisfy themselves that the  imported  goods answer to the tariff description and meet the conditions of the exemption notification.     Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: Naidu's Amaravati offers a model for ambitious, planned urban development
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Naidu's Amaravati offers a model for ambitious, planned urban developmentNaidu's Amaravati offers a model for ambitious, planned urban development

The Andhra CM's commitment is underlined by the fact that he never abandoned the idea. He promised to revive it and is now building it at warp speed

N Chandrababu Naidu (Photo:PTI)

Shekhar Gupta8 min read Last Updated : Nov 14 2026 | 9:30 AM ISTThis week’s National Interest is datelined Amaravati, the new capital N Chandrababu Naidu is building for Andhra Pradesh, just across the river Krishna from Vijayawada. It isn’t exactly about Amaravati, though. Our central theme is the idea. It’s a novelty in Indian politics, audacious in an era when no politician wants to embark on something she or he cannot complete within one term; or four years, with the fifth reserved for electioneering. Building a Capital takes much longer. One term may not be enough to flaunt it to voters as a success. And what happens if you lose power, as Mr Naidu did in 2019, just after barely collecting his first “pool” of land?  His successor, Y S Jagan Mohan Reddy, and his YSRCP (Yuvajana Sramika Rythu Congress Party) called the project a sham, intended to benefit one caste, Mr Naidu’s own, since most farmers pooling land for the project were fellow Kamma. Mr Reddy scrapped the project, stopped annuity payments to farmers who had contributed their land, and declared that Andhra Pradesh would have three Capitals instead: Vizag as the executive Capital, Amaravati the legislative Capital and Kurnool the judicial Capital. 

Also Read

Jailer 2 and Rajinikanth's vicarious politics: The paradox of a superstarpremium

US midterm upset leaves India facing a tougher regional recalibrationpremium

Andhra Pradesh bags ₹9.98 trillion in investment pledges at CII summit

Agnikul to set up Andhra Pradesh facility for orbital data centre units

ReNew to invest ₹1.6 trn in Andhra over 7 yrs: Chairman & CEO Sumant Sinhapremium

Decentralisation might be an interesting idea, but not like this. Andhra Pradesh is a large state, and the distance between Vizag and Kurnool is about 700 km, with Amaravati (Vijayawada) exactly in the middle. This deserved to be called Tughlaq-like, which I did. And while Mr Reddy and his party leaders remained polite, Sakshi, the newspaper owned by his family, which had Telugu rights to publish National Interest, dropped it. That, however, is a mere sidelight in a serious discourse. Mr Naidu’s commitment is underlined by the fact that he never abandoned the idea. He promised to revive it and is now building it at warp speed. So fast, indeed, that even if there’s a change of government in the future, there will be little left to reverse. The new Capital is becoming a reality faster than electoral fortunes turn. That persistence with such an ambitious, expansive and expensive idea is what makes this project remarkable. The idea of building a new living, political, commercial, hi-tech, cultural and educational city with a soul is unfamiliar to us. We have built sarkari enclaves out of necessity: Gandhinagar, Naya Raipur, even Bhubaneswar. But these are merely seats of government. The only new city independent India has built is Chandigarh, designed for half a million people. It now has perhaps 1.4 million. That’s no city, even if it’s my hometown for all practical purposes. According to a report submitted by the Indian Institute of Human Settlements (IIHS) to the 15th Finance Commission, all cities built since Independence house no more than, hold your breath, 130 million people. These are mostly glorified colonies for ministers, legislators, officials, employees, their families and domestic workers. There’s no commerce, entrepreneurship or culture. For all that, you go to an old city nearby. Building a city, or even significantly upgrading an existing one, is an idea India has been fundamentally averse to. Why invest resources in cities when, as Gandhi told us, India lives in its villages? Those villages are so rotten in terms of quality of life, so short of opportunity and so socially unequal that millions have been leaving them for cities. Yet planned spending on cities, whether the hundreds we inherited, some dating back millennia, or those that grew chaotically into urban sprawls, was seen as a waste and a political liability. That’s why even existing cities, without exception, have decayed over time. Meanwhile, India urbanised as millions left their villages for these same cities, mostly settling in slums that the mafia gradually came to control. What’s called a slum in Mumbai goes by the name of “unauthorised colonies” in Delhi, which every political party promises to legalise. Residents are condemned to live in the same muck, with open drains. Overhanging wires and cables across the streets make them resemble a rainforest, though one made of plastic. Mumbai has been avidly cannibalising its decrepit old mills and slums. The good thing is that it’s finally building a subcity, Navi Mumbai, with the Trans-Harbour Link connecting the island city to the mainland. It’s a work in progress. Delhi employed the lazier ploy of letting large suburbs come up in Gurugram and Noida, creating a commuting and traffic nightmare as vehicles travel long distances between the three.  A large majority of Delhi’s population, however, continues to live in subhuman conditions in its unauthorised colonies. Sanjay Gandhi gave these settlements a cute name: JJ colonies, or jhuggi-jhopdi (slum and hutment). Many have been partly gentrified over time, with minimal, if any, municipal facilities. Satya Niketan, where a building collapse in September killed seven students, is one such. Bengaluru has expanded haphazardly, with the world’s worst connectivity between its city centre and economic engines. It gets flooded up to the second floor in some of its richest colonies and thirsts for water the rest of the year. The tanker mafia rules India’s Silicon Valley. And what do we say about Kolkata? Barring some new developments on the outskirts, it’s difficult to describe anything there as a slum. Most of its population still lives with a similar quality of life. Just one major Indian city bucked this trend, and it wasn’t yet a metro. Hyderabad woke up to add the muscle of tech entrepreneurship to its soul and historic spirit. It was Mr Naidu who started this during his first of four chief ministerships, beginning in 1995. He founded Cyberabad to compete with Bengaluru. His successor, Y S Rajasekhara Reddy of the Congress, carried that Telugu entrepreneurship forward, and built on it. The city didn’t just survive political change, it thrived.Mr Naidu was told by many, including much of our ‘old school’ socialist commentariat, that he had erred by focusing on the city, playing chief executive officer of the state and ignoring the poor in the process. His persistence with Amaravati, despite the 2019 electoral setback, is now seen as evidence that he’s incorrigible. And it’s a good thing. To repeat, this column isn’t about Amaravati. That deserves a full episode of “Writings On The Wall” sometime later. But a few points, especially its innovation in urbanisation, deserve mention. The biggest challenge to building infrastructure in our country is land acquisition. How come there were minimal protests in Amaravati? Mr Naidu’s first innovation was his land-pooling scheme. Farmers were invited to pool their land instead of selling it. For every acre, he committed to returning a share in developed residential and commercial plots. And what would farmers do until the Capital was built and the land monetised? Mr Naidu promised an annuity, starting at ₹50,000 per acre annually, with a 5 per cent increase every year. Today it is ₹95,000, far more than what any farmer earns from an acre. About 33,000 acres were pooled this way. The government added another 20,000 acres of its own around the planned city, taking its total area to about 53,000 acres or 217.23 square km. It’s a planned city, with grids neatly dividing it into blocks of 1 square km. Best of all, the entire government — offices, ministers, legislators, the High Court, the Vidhan Sabha and the Legislative Council, and employees of all classes — will be housed along a 7-km-long central median, occupying just 7 square km. The rest will be developed privately, with universities, tech hubs and an IBM Quantum Hub (120-qubit to begin with), scheduled for inauguration next February. This is important because governments usually consume every vacant piece of land available. Here, the government owns no more than these 7 square km. This is the second innovation. The third is a kind of political insurance. What if someone invests on the strength of your promised incentives and you lose power? Mr Naidu passed a law this week to protect investment and ensure that a share of the taxes received from these entrepreneurs went into escrow accounts, with mandatory payouts on committed dates. It’s around these political and administrative innovations that he is building this trillion-rupee city. It’s a good example for other chief ministers. Take some risks and, as he says, create wealth so the government can earn more and distribute it.

entry.title: US midterms deepen uncertainty over future policy and ties with India
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / US midterms deepen uncertainty over future policy and ties with IndiaUS midterms deepen uncertainty over future policy and ties with India

Trump's midterm defeat may not change his policy direction, while a future Democratic administration may also retain elements of his inward-looking approach

premium

US President Donald Trump | Image: Bloomberg

Mihir S Sharma4 min read Last Updated : Nov 13 2026 | 11:02 PM ISTIn the United States (US), it is common for the party of the incumbent President to lose seats in the legislature in the election cycle that comes two years after the presidential elections, the so-called midterms. But, even given this history, the scale of the defeat suffered by the Republican Party of President Donald Trump is staggering. In some parts of the country, and among some groups of voters, the aggregate swing in vote share towards the opposition Democratic Party was in excess of 40 per cent. These are very large numbers.  The question now is what this implies for US policy going forward, particularly to those aspects of it — foreign affairs, technology regulation, and so on — which impact their relationship with the rest of the world, and especially India. That question, in turn, resolves into three. First, how will the incumbent President respond over the course of his remaining term to this defeat? Second, how much will his successor in the Republican Party diverge from Mr Trump’s approach? And third, do the Democrats provide a substantively different way of thinking about these problems in a way that would impact decision-making in non-American Capitals?  The President himself, it appears, has chosen to not see this defeat as a rebuke to himself personally. He has repeatedly said that he was “not on the ticket”, meaning that he believes that his party and its candidates are responsible, not his own popularity or lack thereof. This is in spite of the fact that his approval ratings are historically low.  He has also appointed Stephen Miller, a hardliner known best for his negative take on immigration from countries like India, as his new chief of staff. This suggests that, if anything, he will double down on those aspects of his “America-first” agenda. There does not seem to be an increased probability that he   will re-examine his approach to trade policy, for example, or to change his approach to artificial intelligence (AI) and how it is both essentially unregulated and designed to benefit big US-based technology companies.  How will he approach the war in Iran? After all, the decision to bomb Iran and kill its leader — starting a war that he has been so far unable to finish to his satisfaction — is largely responsible for a surge in energy prices and inflationary pressures across the world. According to his own vice-president, J D Vance, this decision bears most of the responsibility for the unprecedented drubbing that the Republicans received across the country. Mr Trump responded on Thursday by taking his vice-president off negotiations with Iran and refocusing him on domestic issues.  If Mr Vance is treated as the frontrunner to be the next leader of the Republican Party, an even more inward-looking US is probably on the cards — if one that is less committed to disruptive wars. If, instead, Secretary of State Marco Rubio emerges as the primary candidate, then the US might return to a more familiar, muscular approach to defence — but with the addition of strong export controls to manage and manipulate tech-supply chains. But then again, it might be an outsider with a somewhat more confrontational approach to Big Tech than the Silicon Valley-funded Mr Vance. Florida’s outgoing governor, Ron DeSantis, has been touring the country, asking for as much.  With the triumphant Democrats, it is far harder to sense what their shift in approach to the world might be if they recapture power. Obviously the war in Iran will end, and there may be no more such adventures. But will they maintain Mr Trump’s tendency to withdrawing from the world in terms of trade and multilateralism? Will they commit themselves to restoring alliances and to restoring deterrence over such issues as the Taiwan Strait? Will they view China as a competitor, and, if so, how will they treat countries in the Indo-Pacific, including India?  The fact is that, while Mr Trump’s first term marked a major departure from the previous decades of American leadership in the world, his Democratic successor did not completely reverse course. That administration continued the inward turn, including through the botched and immoral withdrawal from Afghanistan, and made it bipartisan. There is every chance that, as far as the rest of the world is concerned, the Democratic successor, if there is one, to Mr Trump will not change as much as we would like.     Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: Jailer 2 and Rajinikanth's vicarious politics: The paradox of a superstar
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Jailer 2 and Rajinikanth's vicarious politics: The paradox of a superstarJailer 2 and Rajinikanth's vicarious politics: The paradox of a superstar

Rajinikanth's career presents a paradox. An actor who began by defying conventions gradually became captive to a persona that demanded repetition

premium

Subashini K J J5 min read Last Updated : Nov 13 2026 | 10:53 PM ISTHe is 75 going on 76, but Rajinikanth’s superstar status in Tamil cinema remains unshaken. Jailer 2 is yet another proof of that. The film has become the highest-grossing Tamil movie of all time, amassing over ₹700 crore within 11 days of its release. How the actor has managed to hold the audience for over half a century is a question that has no one answer.  The legendary director K Balachander had foreseen this phenomenon as early as the 1970s, the late playback singer S P Balasubrahmanyam once narrated: “When we were in the AVM studio (in Chennai), he (Balachander) asked me to turn around and look at the person sitting behind us.” Balasubrahmanyam said while he found nothing extraordinary about this person, Balachander prophesied that the “dark man with unkempt hair sitting behind us would rule Tamil cinema for at least the next 30 years”. The man he was pointing to was Rajinikanth. Many had underestimated the actor, given that most of his contemporaries were fair-skinned heroes.  Rajinikanth, who made a brief appearance in Balachander’s Apoorva Raagangal (1975) as the leading lady’s husband, would go on to rule Tamil cinema. He started out with small but striking roles, often playing the bad guy, including in films starring Kamal Haasan. In Pathinaaru Vayathinile (1977), for instance, he enacts a village thug who covets Sridevi, but she is in love with Chappani (Kamal Haasan). He excelled in negative roles before allowing himself to give in to the demands of his own larger-than-life image.  Of course, the brands came calling. Why wouldn’t they? But the actor refused to endorse any, with the exception of Palm Cola, a state government initiative for a regional soft drink produced by the Tamil Nadu State Palmgur and Fibre Marketing Cooperative Federation, in the early 1980s. The cooperative provided support to local palm tree climbers.  Also, unlike other super successful actors such as M G Ramachandran (MGR), Jayalalithaa, and now C Joseph Vijay, he has steered clear of politics. Whatever politics he engages in begins and ends with the films he stars in, such as Jailer 2.  That’s not to say he is apolitical. Far from it.  In the mid-1990s, when Jayalalithaa was Tamil Nadu chief minister and when few public figures dared to openly challenge her, he voiced his concern over the law-and-order situation in the state. This was after a bomb was hurled at the residence of filmmaker Mani Ratnam in Chennai after the release of Bombay.  The incident had triggered widespread anxiety, and Rajinikanth’s public criticism carried considerable weight.  R M Veerappan, a minister from Jayalalithaa’s cabinet, was present on the dais when the actor spoke up.  The episode fuelled speculation about Rajinikanth’s political ambitions. But the actor repeatedly hesitated to take the plunge. In the 1996 Assembly election, he openly backed the Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK)-Tamil Maanila Congress (TMC) alliance led by G K Moopanar. His endorsement was seen as a significant factor that helped the alliance defeat the All India Anna Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (AIADMK). Thereafter, speculation about his entry into politics became a recurring theme in Tamil Nadu. Every statement, every public appearance or film release was scrutinised for clues. For years, the question was: Would he; wouldn’t he?  Meanwhile, his films increasingly reinforced the view that he might.  Dialogues, songs, and title cards carried political undertones; and the stories celebrated a protagonist who could challenge the powerful, defend the downtrodden, and command unquestioning loyalty. Films such as Baashha, Annamalai, Padayappa, and Ejamaan helped consolidate this persona. Later films, too, such as Kaala, Kabali, Coolie, and  Vettaiyan drew upon the superstar’s enormous clout to garner support for Dalit political ideology even as the actor occasionally sought to explore different shades of his screen presence.  Now who better to sum up the phenomenon called Rajinikanth than Rajinikanth himself. In the climax of Jailer 2, the superstar says: “For 50 years, so many people in so many different ways have tried to finish me… but nobody could!”  The irony, though, is that the political authority projected on screen never translated into a political career off it. Rajinikanth can still command the attention of millions through a single dialogue or a gesture, but he could not bring himself to convert that adulation into a political movement of his own.  After years of anticipation, in December 2017, he did announce his decision to launch a political party and contest the Assembly election. However, in December 2020, after falling ill, he decided against it, and chose instead to stick with the world that knows him best: Cinema.  Rajinikanth’s career thus presents a curious paradox. An actor who began by defying conventions gradually became captive to a persona that demanded repetition.  A man whose political interventions once electrified Tamil Nadu never became a politician himself.  The screen gave him the power to rule a fictional world; outside it, he remained hesitant to claim a place in the uncertain world of politics.
