entry.title: As inflation stays elevated, RBI's Dec repo rate increase appears certain
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / As inflation stays elevated, RBI's Dec repo rate increase appears certainAs inflation stays elevated, RBI's Dec repo rate increase appears certain

The MPC in October had projected the retail-inflation rate at 6 per cent for this quarter and 5.7 per cent for the next

premium

Reserve Bank of India (Photo: Reuters)

Business Standard Editorial Comment4 min read Last Updated : Nov 15 2026 | 10:09 PM ISTThe data released by the National Statistics Office last week showed that the consumer price index-based inflation rate stood at 6.09 per cent in October, breaching the upper end of the Reserve Bank of India’s (RBI’s) tolerance band. The rate was at 5.54 per cent in the previous month. An analysis by this newspaper showed that the rate had increased for 12 straight months after bottoming out at 0.04 per cent in October 2025. In October 2026, the food-inflation rate, at about 9 per cent, was the key driver of the headline rate though the core rate too inched up. Inflation pressure is likely to persist in the coming months. Almost all economists agree that the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) of the RBI will increase the policy repo rate by another 25 basis points in its December meeting, following a 25-basis point increase in the October meeting to 5.5 per cent.  The MPC in October had projected the retail-inflation rate at 6 per cent for this quarter and 5.7 per cent for the next. The rate was projected at 5.6 per cent for the first quarter of 2027-28. The latest inflation print has pushed the real repo rate into negative territory, making a policy-rate adjustment necessary. The extent of adjustment in the December meeting and later will depend on several factors, such as the inflation projection for next financial year, prospects of second-order effects through higher food prices, and the level of the real policy rate the central bank is willing to maintain at this stage.  An earlier study by RBI economists had estimated the neutral rate — the real policy rate that is neither expansionary nor contractionary— at 1.4-1.9 per cent. It is possible that it has changed. Even assuming that the RBI is comfortable maintaining the real policy rate at 1-1.25 per cent, the repo rate needs to be adjusted by 50-75 basis points, given that the central bank expects the inflation rate to average 5 per cent in 2027-28, according to its latest biannual Monetary Policy Report (October). However, much depends on possible shifts in inflation projections. The monsoon season ended with a rainfall deficit of about 13 per cent as against the long-period average. Given the expected strong El Niño conditions, with adverse implications for rain in winter and lower reservoir levels, agricultural output could also be affected in the rabi season, potentially keeping food prices elevated. However, there is some relief, at least for now, on the external front. There are indications that the United States (US) may not resume the Iran war anytime soon, though US action under President Donald Trump remains unpredictable as ever. For now, prices of crude oil have come down significantly. Although gains for India on inflation will remain limited due to the limited pass-through of higher global prices to retail prices, prospects of a lower current-account deficit will support the currency and reduce its impact on inflation outcomes. Lower oil prices and a selloff in artificial intelligence-related stocks in the US have also brought back foreign portfolio investors. While this development will provide stability to the rupee, the RBI will be well advised to use such opportunities to rebuild its foreign-exchange reserves. Stability on the external front will also allow the RBI to focus on inflation management. While the consensus is that the MPC will increase the repo rate by 25 basis points in the December meeting, it may even consider a 50-basis point rate increase to send a strong message, given that growth is not a concern at the moment.   Topics : Inflation RBI retail inflation CPI Inflation repo rate Business Standard Editorial Comment Editorial Comment

entry.title: Nvidia's dominance and succession risks expose fragility in the AI boom
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Nvidia's dominance and succession risks expose fragility in the AI boomNvidia's dominance and succession risks expose fragility in the AI boom

Nvidia clawed its way up from being a specialist in graphics co-processors to become the dominant player in gaming, and then in AI

premium

Nvidia, which was until recently the most valuable company in the world, provides the most crucial component of the hardware infrastructure underpinning the global artificial intelligence (AI) boom

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Nov 16 2026 | 12:24 AM ISTGlobal stock markets are assessing a situation that management theorists describe as “concentration risk”. The exit of Jensen Huang, who was reportedly honey-trapped, as chief executive officer of Nvidia has created considerable uncertainty about the company’s future. Nvidia, which was until recently the most valuable company in the world, provides the most crucial component of the hardware infrastructure underpinning the global artificial intelligence (AI) boom. More broadly, Nvidia holds a dominant market share across the rest of the information technology (IT) industry, and enjoys monopoly status in graphics-intensive spaces such as gaming. Nvidia did not have a succession plan because Mr Jensen did not believe in one. About 60 departments reported directly to him. This may have worked well to accelerate the pace of strategic decisions. But the lack of a formal succession plan means that the Nvidia board must face the challenges of appointing a capable team. That team must develop and articulate a consistent business strategy, and restore investor confidence in a $4 trillion company. Moreover, Nvidia faces investigations from multiple agencies of the United States (US) government and will likely be forced to answer questions in the US Congress. The leadership vacuum has also led Wall Street to suddenly focus on a possible financial weakness in Nvidia’s circular sales strategy. The chipmaker has an excellent credit rating and deploys that to help customers who need to raise debt to buy its chips. The Nvidia balance sheet discloses that it has over $108 billion in outstanding credit guarantees resulting from this circular strategy. One high-profile deal involves selling chips to Oracle, which has debt guarantees from Nvidia. Oracle will use those chips to set up data centres that OpenAI will run. The concentration risks are, therefore, evident. Nvidia holds a dominant share in critical market segments and, if it stumbles operationally, there would be slowdowns across broad swathes of the digital economy. If, in addition, financial issues arise with its guarantees and the circular model blows up, the sums involved are big enough to trigger a crisis across global financial markets. To use an oft-abused phrase, Nvidia may genuinely be too big to fail. And yet, history is not on its side.  It operates in the most hi-tech hardware segment, and no company has maintained dominance for too long in that segment. In prior cycles, IBM, Intel and AMD dominated the chip landscape. Nvidia clawed its way up from being a specialist in graphics co-processors to become the dominant player in gaming, and then in AI. (A co-processor is a chip that runs number-intensive calculations, leaving the main processor in a computer free to do other things.) Google is using its internally designed TPUs (tensor processing units) and intends to start selling and leasing them out. China, officially deprived of access to Nvidia technology, is said to be developing alternatives. But there will be a gap in the market until such alternatives are available in industrial quantities. If Nvidia cannot put a succession plan in place, deal with investigations, sell the succession plan to investors, and navigate the circular financing situation, the exit of one man could result in a cascade of disastrous consequences. The AI bubble is currently deflating, with Nvidia being one of the triggers. If the bubble pops instead of reverting gradually to rational valuations, it could lead to substantial volatility in financial markets if not a full-blown crisis.   Topics : Artificial intelligence Nvidia industry stock markets Global stock markets Business Standard Editorial Comment Editorial Comment

entry.title: Factory safety must underpin India's manufacturing ambitions and investment
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Factory safety must underpin India's manufacturing ambitions and investmentFactory safety must underpin India's manufacturing ambitions and investment

More significantly, 338 fatal injuries attributed to gassing were recorded over 2014-23, indicating that such incidents are neither new nor unfamiliar

premium

Hazardous operations must be subject to mandatory risk assessments, confined-space entry permits, gas monitoring, emergency rescue arrangements, and regular independent audits

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Nov 12 2026 | 10:35 PM ISTThe death of three contract workers from asphyxiation at Tata Electronics’ Hosur facility in Tamil Nadu, which manufactures components for Apple’s iPhones, raises serious questions about safety in India’s manufacturing sector. The workers, engaged through a subcontractor, reportedly died while cleaning an effluent-treatment tank. The incident is particularly concerning, given that three workers died while cleaning a sewage tank at a dyeing unit in Tiruppur in May 2025. The recurrence of such accidents points to persistent weaknesses in workplace safety practices. Cleaning industrial tanks and other confined spaces requires prior risk assessment, gas testing, adequate ventilation, appropriate protective equipment, and trained persons equipped to handle emergencies. The Hosur incident also raises questions about fragmented accountability in large manufacturing establishments, where maintenance and ancillary operations are frequently outsourced through multiple layers of contractors. While the workers were employed by a subcontractor, the principal manufacturing establishment cannot treat workplace safety as an issue entirely external to its operations.  India’s record on industrial accidents reinforces these concerns. According to the Directorate General Factory Advice Service and Labour Institutes (DGFASLI), registered factories reported 1,090 fatal injuries in 2023. More significantly, 338 fatal injuries attributed to gassing were recorded over 2014-23, indicating that such incidents are neither new nor unfamiliar. Enforcement capacity is another concern. In 2023, India had 630 working factory inspectors against 974 sanctioned positions. The four Labour Codes, which came into force in November 2025, provide a framework for addressing some of these shortcomings. The Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020, places broad obligations on employers to maintain safe workplaces and protect workers from occupational hazards. Importantly, its provisions extend beyond directly employed personnel to cover contract labour. However, statutory provisions alone cannot prevent accidents. Their effectiveness depends on inspection, enforcement and accountability across contractor and subcontractor arrangements.  The consequences of such incidents extend beyond worker safety. India has been positioning itself as an alternative manufacturing destination as multinational companies diversify production beyond China. Apple’s expanding Indian supply chain, in particular, represents an important opportunity to integrate domestic manufacturers into global value chains. However, repeated incidents involving factory fires, labour disputes, environmental violations and workplace fatalities can affect perceptions of operational reliability. Accidents can disrupt production, increase compliance and insurance costs, invite regulatory scrutiny, and expose multinational companies to reputational risks. It is incorrect to assume that fiscal incentives and lower production costs alone will secure India’s position in global manufacturing networks.  Hazardous operations must be subject to mandatory risk assessments, confined-space entry permits, gas monitoring, emergency rescue arrangements, and regular independent audits. Greater mechanisation of dangerous cleaning and maintenance activities can also reduce workers’ exposure to preventable risks. Strengthening factory-inspection capacity and improving the reporting of industrial accidents are equally important. Thus, worker safety is not merely a matter of corporate responsibility or labour regulation; it is integral to productivity, operational continuity, and investment confidence.     Topics : workplace safety Manufacturing sector Tata Supply chain Business Standard Editorial Comment Editorial Comment

entry.title: Coal gasification ecosystem needs assured demand to attract investment
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Coal gasification ecosystem needs assured demand to attract investmentCoal gasification ecosystem needs assured demand to attract investment

Weak response to the coal-gasification scheme highlights commercial viability concerns, underscoring the need for assured demand, easier financing, indigenous technology and better infrastructure

premium

Coal gasification requires substantial upfront investment, and the projects have long gestation periods and involve considerable technological complexity

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Nov 12 2026 | 10:27 PM ISTThe tepid response to the second round of the ₹37,500 crore coal-gasification scheme exposes the gap between policy ambition and commercial viability. The scheme envisages supporting 25 projects, but the second round attracted just two applications, both from state-owned NTPC. This compares poorly with seven applications in the first round from five companies, including Adani Enterprises, Talcher Fertilisers, Gallantt Ispat and Shyam Sel & Power. The response is a setback for the government’s ambition to gasify 75 million tonnes of coal by 2030 under the scheme, contributing to the broader national target of gasifying 100 million tonnes of coal. The strategic importance of the scheme is clear. With about 389 billion tonnes of coal reserves, among the world’s largest, India has a substantial domestic resource base that can be used beyond power generation. The push for gasification is important, given India’s ₹2.77 trillion import bill for liquefied natural gas (LNG), urea, ammonia and methanol in FY25. Coal gasification could help diversify feedstock sources for fertilisers and chemicals, reduce exposure to international price volatility, and strengthen industrial supply chains. The government expects the scheme to mobilise ₹2.5 trillion-3 trillion in investment and generate around 50,000 direct and indirect jobs.  Yet the limited response suggests that capital support alone may not be sufficient. Coal gasification requires substantial upfront investment, and the projects have long gestation periods and involve considerable technological complexity. Their economics are also sensitive to international prices. When imported natural gas and chemicals are cheaper, domestic syngas and its derivatives may struggle to compete mainly due to a lack of assured buyers. Uncertainty over long-term coal supplies, transportation infrastructure and the availability of specialised plant machinery further complicates investment decisions. There are also environmental considerations that cannot be overlooked. Gasification is not inherently a low-carbon alternative to conventional coal use. The process can generate substantial carbon emission and requires significant water, making it particularly challenging in coal-bearing regions facing water stress. Integrating with carbon capture, utilisation and storage (CCUS) will, therefore, be important in limiting its environmental footprint.  The immediate priority should be to improve the commercial viability of projects. Long-term purchase agreements for syngas and downstream products are critical. Public-sector companies in the fertiliser, energy and chemical industries could anchor demand through assured procurement arrangements. The government could also consider a partial credit-guarantee mechanism to share lending risks, lower borrowing costs, and improve access to finance. Including coal gasification in the harmonised list of infrastructure sub-sectors could further facilitate long-term financing. Equally important is developing indigenous technology. Collaboration among public-sector enterprises, research institutions and private companies should be encouraged to scale up domestic technologies.  The progress made by Bharat Heavy Electricals Ltd in developing gasification technology suited to India’s high-ash coal offers a foundation to build on. These could develop confidence in other domestic companies to apply for the third round, which the Centre has opened now. The government has extended coal-linkage tenure to 30 years for the syngas and gasification sub-sector, an important step towards providing supply certainty. However, this needs to be complemented by better logistics and demand visibility.     Topics : Coal Coal ministry Indian Economy infrastructure Business Standard Editorial Comment Editorial Comment

entry.title: Groundwater recharge needs local action and changes to farming practices
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Groundwater recharge needs local action and changes to farming practicesGroundwater recharge needs local action and changes to farming practices

El Niño and below-normal rainfall heighten pressure on India's groundwater reserves, underscoring the need to combine scientific recharge planning with efficient irrigation and crop diversification.

premium

India needs scientific groundwater recharge planning, efficient irrigation and crop diversification to address declining water reserves and protect farmers' livelihoods.

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Nov 11 2026 | 10:23 PM ISTEl Nino has raised fresh concern about higher temperatures, erratic rain, and pressure on India’s groundwater reserves. The India Meteorological Department (IMD) recorded 759.4 mm of rainfall during the June-September monsoon, 12.6 per cent below the long-period average. The IMD’s latest outlook shows below-normal rain across most parts of the country in November, alongside above-normal maximum temperatures. Very strong El Nino conditions are expected to persist through November-December. This raises concern about irrigation demand and water availability as India enters the cropping season in winter. Farmers are again likely to turn to groundwater.  The Central Ground Water Board’s 2025 assessment highlighted the structural problems associated with excessive dependence on groundwater. India’s annual groundwater recharge was estimated at 448.52 billion cubic metres (BCM) while extractable resources stood at 407.75 BCM. Annual extraction reached 247.22 BCM, equivalent to 60.63 per cent of the available extractable amount. The assessment classified 730 units as over-exploited, where extraction exceeds replenishment. Agriculture accounts for nearly 87 per cent of groundwater extraction, often in regions where water is scarce, making conservation as important as replenishment.  Against this backdrop, the Ministry of Jal Shakti’s newly launched Punah Bharan mobile application and web portal are a welcome step towards building longer-term solutions. The application uses geospatial data on rainfall, groundwater levels, yields, slopes and drainage to identify potential artificial recharge zones within a radius of up to 3 kilometres. It also recommends suitable recharge structures based on local conditions. The accompanying web portal provides village-level maps and geographic information system tools. These tools can help local authorities identify suitable locations for recharge and direct public investment for interventions that are more likely to be effective.  However, technology must lead to action through trained local staff, watershed programmes and village-level water budgets. A 2025 study of managed aquifer recharge in the Ramganga basin found that existing programmes contributed an estimated 255 million cubic metres to groundwater storage in 2023, equivalent to only 2.5-7.5 per cent of rainfall recharge. Despite these efforts, groundwater levels continued to decline. The study underlines the need to combine recharge infrastructure with efficient irrigation and crop diversification. Micro-irrigation, less water-intensive crops, and regulating excessive extraction must complement recharge efforts. Ultimately, recharge investment will deliver lasting benefits only if farmers have both the means and the incentive to protect the aquifers on which their livelihoods depend. An assured procurement of less water-intensive crops, insurance, and access to markets can reduce the risks of diversification. Agricultural extension services can help translate these measures into practice by guiding farmers on irrigation scheduling, water-saving technologies, and suitable crop choices. This support is particularly important for small and marginal farmers, who often lack the resources and technical assistance to change established practices. As one of the world’s largest groundwater users, India must make recharge planning part of a broader effort to secure long-term water resources and livelihoods.   Topics : Groundwater levels BS Opinion Business Standard Editorial Comment El Nino water reservoirs Water scarcity

entry.title: Airtel's restored entry tariff highlights telcos' revenue-growth dilemma
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Airtel's restored entry tariff highlights telcos' revenue-growth dilemmaAirtel's restored entry tariff highlights telcos' revenue-growth dilemma

Indian telecom operators face the challenge of raising average revenue per user (Arpu) while retaining subscribers, as pressure to increase tariffs runs up against affordability and competition.

premium

Indian telecom operators face the challenge of raising average revenue per user (Arpu) while retaining subscribers, as pressure to increase tariffs runs up against affordability and competition.

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Nov 11 2026 | 10:18 PM ISTIn an unusual reversal, Bharti Airtel brought back an entry-level prepaid recharge plan that had been withdrawn just a few months ago. The recent return of the ₹299-per month tariff plan proves the challenge facing the telecom industry in increasing revenue. In August, the telco removed this tariff plan in an effort to move entry-level customers to a higher slab, thereby trying to push up the monthly average revenue per user (Arpu). When the move, coupled with higher prices and a slower shipment of entry-level smartphones, resulted in a subscriber churn and a sharp dip in customer additions, the Sunil Bharti Mittal-led company reinstated the plan while marginally reducing the data usage available under the scheme.     Striking a balance between subscriber numbers and Arpu, a key metric indicating a service provider’s health, has been a tough call for the industry known for its low tariffs. With its launch in 2016, Airtel’s rival Reliance Jio disrupted the telecom market. Since then, steps to rationalise tariffs have been few, keeping Arpu stuck below ₹200 a month for years. While telcos have in the past dismissed the relevance of subscriber numbers and the pecking order in terms of volume, the latest example goes against that notion. The message sent out by Airtel is that subscribers cannot be sacrificed at any cost, even as it remains emphatic about other levers of growth such as tariff plan upgrades, post-paid service, top-ups and international roaming to meet the goal of a substantially higher Arpu.  The leadership at Airtel, which has maintained the importance of a higher Arpu for the telecom industry to make a mark globally, saw the company’s monthly Arpu at ₹271 during the second quarter of 2026-27, as against ₹218.8 of Reliance Jio, the biggest telco in terms of consumer numbers. Earlier this year, Mr Mittal set an ambitious target of raising the industry’s Arpu to ₹350, without stating a timeline. To achieve that goal, however, telcos will have to explore the way forward on tariff rationalisation. Reliance Jio, which was listed on the stock exchanges last month, is expected to move towards a higher Arpu over the next few months. Reliance Jio Managing Director Akash Ambani said recently that the company had the option of increasing mobile tariffs but would drive revenue growth through more services rather than higher data prices. Vodafone Idea, the third private telco of the country, has been in talks with banks for debt financing. Any industry initiative towards tariff rationalisation will help Vodafone Idea, in which the government holds a stake of over 49 per cent, to reduce its losses and liabilities.  With the focus on revenue, the Cellular Operators Association of India (COAI), which represents telcos, recently wrote to the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (Trai), pushing for higher interconnection charges for international calls. By Trai’s definition, interconnection is the bedrock of any multi-operator telecom environment, ensuring that subscribers of one network can seamlessly communicate with those on another. The COAI cited the erosion of earnings due to currency depreciation for seeking higher termination charges. On its part, the government has taken several steps in recent years to prevent the telecom industry from slipping into a duopoly and maintain a reasonable level of competition. Now the companies need to proactively focus on revenues for a better telecom future, which will also enable better-quality services for subscribers.   Topics : Bharti Airtel Telecom Bharti Airtel plans Reliance Jio BS Opinion Business Standard Editorial Comment Telecom industry

entry.title: Nvidia turmoil links Huang's scandal to AI markets and geopolitics
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Nvidia turmoil links Huang's scandal to AI markets and geopoliticsNvidia turmoil links Huang's scandal to AI markets and geopolitics

Nvidia's leadership uncertainty, alleged geopolitical links and circular AI funding raise questions about the future of the AI boom

premium

Jensen Huang | Image: Bloomberg

Devangshu Datta New Delhi 4 min read Last Updated : Nov 13 2026 | 10:46 PM ISTIt is a truth empirically evident that a middle-aged tech maven in possession of a fortune running into billions is likely to be involved in an extra marital relationship. Exhibit A: Jensen Huang. It also happened to Bill Gates, Jeff Bezos, Sergey Brin and Elon Musk, among others. Mr Jensen’s affairs, however, may be more consequential than the peccadillos of the others mentioned above. One reason is the geopolitical implications. Another is the management structure of Nvidia, the company he led until two days ago, and its artificial intelligence-critical status.  The others went through divorces and settlements, which put (barely perceptible) dents in their fortunes. The many former Mrs Musks and their multitude of kids are said to eke out their lives with complex resource-sharing arrangements, managed by a legion of support staff and artificial intelligence (of course!). The Bezos divorce led to a big uptick in global philanthropy. The former Mrs Bezos, Mackenzie Scott, makes enormous contributions to various causes. Melinda Gates focuses on The Gates Foundation, and works with her former husband on projects.   Those divorces made no difference to the companies the above-mentioned billionaires founded. Microsoft, Tesla, Amazon, SpaceX and Alphabet saw zero glitches in daily functioning, and no reworking of corporate structures. The companies continued to record profits and generate much wealth for investors, including the adulterers and their ex-es.  But in Nvidia’s case, the liaison of Mr Jensen with Alice Huang Le (no relation) is being described as the “affair that cost a trillion”, with a less polite synonym for “affair” being deployed. It has also been categorised as “the p***k that deflated the AI (artificial intelligence) bubble”, by Wall Street analysts who appear to be doubling as punsters.  There’s been a global bloodbath in AI and AI-adjacent shares. Nvidia’s market value has been shaved off by $900 billion and counting. Other companies with AI-related valuations have seen deep selloffs in sideswipes by bears. Anthropic’s initial public offering may go through with Claude’s creator valued at a mere $1.5 trillion, instead of the $2 trillion-plus earlier assumed. The Huang revelation was coincident with the overwhelming victory of the Democratic Party in the United States midterm elections, where multiple candidates ran on anti-data-centre platforms. It now appears likely that guardrails and controls, including regulatory control of research and stringent environmental oversight, will be imposed. The breakneck pace of investment in AI infrastructure will slow.  When a gold rush starts, it is hard to spot the miners who will strike it rich. But the manufacturers of the pickaxes are guaranteed winners. Nvidia makes the chips that enable number-crunching for AI. The returns have been dizzying as Nvidia has become a multi-trillion-dollar company due to its technological edge. Those chips are so critical to compute that there’s been a running battle in the US administration to stop their export to China.  Mr Jensen is close to the US President and hence was in a position to influence those decisions. Alice Huang is allegedly a Chinese intelligence asset. She runs a Singapore-based company, Megaspeed, which is said to be funded by Mainland China. She may have helped China gain access to Nvidia chips and technology.  The geopolitical implications from that tangle of relationships among the White House, Nvidia, and Alice-Jensen may be considerable.  There are also nervous palpitations as the circular nature of some AI-related funding is apparent. Nvidia currently offers financial guarantees of over $108 billion to companies that buy its chips. Also, take a look at the relationships among Oracle, OpenAI and Nvidia. Oracle buys chips to set up data centres. OpenAI commits to owning and using data centres. The chips are bought with debt that may be guaranteed by Nvidia, which is also a co-signer and guarantor on a $250 billion data-centre plan by OpenAI.    Mr Jensen ran Nvidia alone with over 40 departments directly reporting to him. This worked brilliantly while he was there. How that structure will be reworked is a big question. He (along with spouse Lori) is also the fourth-largest shareholder with a stake of around 3.6 per cent, amounting to 800 million shares. Even after the selloff that’s worth over $130 billion. All Nvidia equity consists of voting shares and the company’s structure was such that the 11-member board needed only a majority resolution to sack him. Until there’s a clear succession plan, and until the geopolitical tangle is unravelled (or quietly buried), Nvidia’s stock could continue its deep dive. Investors are wondering what it might drag down in its wake.  
The writer is a New Delhi-based independent journalist   Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. They do not necessarily reflect the opinion of www.business-standard.com or the Business Standard newspaperTopics : Artificial intelligence Nvidia technology industry

entry.title: US midterm upset leaves India facing a tougher regional recalibration
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / US midterm upset leaves India facing a tougher regional recalibrationUS midterm upset leaves India facing a tougher regional recalibration

Since a US President enjoys immense executive powers, American foreign policy may not witness any significant change as a result of the elections

premium

Illustration: Binay Sinha

Shyam Saran6 min read Last Updated : Nov 13 2026 | 10:40 PM ISTThe Democratic Party has swept the November 4 midterm polls in the United States (US) and now it controls both the Senate and the House of Representatives. This is a resounding rejection of domestic and external policies pursued by US President Donald Trump during the first two years of his four-year tenure. In a moment of candour, Vice-President J D Vance cited four key reasons for the political turnaround: The failure to end the Iran war; the cost of living and inflation; an inadequate implementation of “America First” policies; and the changing relationship with Israel. Mr Vance added that what proved decisive was the Iran war.  To his list may be added the reverse swing of support away from the Republican Party among Latino voters and other minorities. There were local factors in several states, in particular the opposition to the building of energy- and water-guzzling data centres, which are required to sustain the headlong rush to develop frontier artificial-intelligence (AI) models. Democratic candidates, particularly from its left-leaning Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) wing, were able to tap into the revulsion against the super-rich, the rising inequality of wealth and income, and anger over the pervasive and blatant nepotism and corruption among Mr Trump’s family members and privileged associates. These added up to a perfect storm. Is this a historic turning point in US politics? One should be cautious in making such judgements. One recalls that when Barack Obama was elected the first black President of the US in 2008, there were similar comments — that the US had entered a post-racial era. And yet the backlash soon came with the election of Mr Trump and the open avowal of white supremacist sentiments. To go back to Mr Vance’s post-mortem, what is striking is the negativity towards Israel, which is now shared by both the right and left peripheries of the political spectrum in the US. Israel may be the biggest loser in this election though its value as an American proxy in the region may remain largely unaffected. American support may, henceforth, be selective, not automatic as it has been so far.  Do Mr Vance’s remarks presage a drawing down and termination of the Iran war? Mr Trump remains unpredictable. He may escalate the war or he could exit after declaring victory. The appointment of a hardliner like Stephen Miller to the key position of White House chief of staff does not augur well. What may bring restraint are prospects of rising prices of oil and gas in case hostilities break out. The US’s Gulf allies, who would be the biggest losers in any resumption of war, are also working hard to broker a US-Iran agreement to end the war. They are working on a parallel track with Iran to discuss regional security architecture with Iran as a key component. But Iran wants the US presence in the region to be removed as a price for such an agreement. How this story plays out should be watched carefully in India, which has major stakes in the region in terms of energy security, the safety and welfare of the nine million-strong Indian diaspora spread across the region, and, most importantly, the security of its entire western maritime flank. A reconfiguration of security equations, with the possibility of the US retrenching its overwhelming military deployments in the region, may create space for a larger Chinese presence and/or a larger role of the Makkah Pact countries — Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan — back-stopped by the US. India had bet on Israel as its key partner in the region. This may need a rethink in view of Israel’s diminished profile in US calculations and its badly damaged reputation in Europe, thanks to its genocidal assaults on Palestinian people. A change of government in Tel Aviv is unlikely to see a material change in this situation.  Despite all the prevailing uncertainty it is clear that Iran has emerged as the most powerful actor in the region. This has been already acknowledged by the Gulf states. To the extent that the Makkah Pact is a virtual alliance against Iran, India has the opportunity to move quickly to establish a strong partnership with Iran as a countervailing move. Given the negative sentiments in Iran against India, thanks to an ill-advised silence over the unprovoked US-Israel attack on Iran, which wiped out its leadership, repairing the relationship will need deft diplomacy, but should be a priority.  One should not expect the blue wave to reverse some of Mr Trump’s hostile measures against India on immigration and on trade. The Democrats are unlikely to ease the limits placed on the entry of Indian professionals into the US. They are equally unlikely to ease up on Mr Trump’s protectionist policies. With the DSA wing in the party gaining greater influence, there may be greater Congressional scrutiny of the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party’s domestic policies on the status of minorities, the limits on political dissent, and alleged human rights violations. The Trump administration has displayed virtually no interest in these matters.  Since a US President enjoys immense executive powers, American foreign policy may not witness any significant change as a result of the elections. However, the election results mean that Mr Trump will play with a weaker hand in his dealings with China and Russia. Some commentators in the US say that the bigger winner of the midterm elections is China. The next meeting between Mr Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping will take place on November 17 and 18 in the Chinese city of Shenzhen, which will be playing host to the summit of the Asia-Pacific Economic Conference. There are reports that there may be a trilateral summit among Mr Trump, Mr Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin. With Mr Xi and Mr Putin on one side, the odds would be stacked against Mr Trump, though he may think that he has the upper hand. The Chinese are playing a game of attrition, chipping away at US security commitment to the defence of Taiwan and eroding US Indo-Pacific strategy to deter China. Mr Putin will seek to gain advantage by playing on divisions between the US and its European allies. In the two years remaining there is a great deal of damage that Mr Trump can inflict on his Western and Asian allies and partners, which a Democratic President, if elected in 2028, will find difficult to reverse. The blue wave may not bring much to cheer about as far as India is concerned.
The writer is a former foreign secretary   Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. They do not necessarily reflect the opinion of www.business-standard.com or the Business Standard newspaperTopics : Donald Trump US midterm elections Peoples Democratic Party BS Opinion

entry.title: Private capital helped build India's early infrastructure, can do so again
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Private capital helped build India's early infrastructure, can do so againPrivate capital helped build India's early infrastructure, can do so again

In 1849, the government offered private companies a guaranteed 5 per cent annual return on the capital they invested to build the railways, backed by free land and licences running up to 100 years

premium

India's first-ever rail passenger service began on April 16, 1853, when the train ran from Bombay (now Mumbai) to Thane

Vinayak Chatterjee5 min read Last Updated : Nov 12 2026 | 10:04 PM ISTOn a spring afternoon in 1853, a 14-carriage train pulled out of Bombay, carrying 400 passengers to Thane, 21 miles away. It is remembered as the birth of the Indian railways. It deserves to be remembered just as much as the birth of Indian private investment in infrastructure because that train was designed, financed and run by a private company. This was nearly a century and a half before “public-private partnership (PPP)” became a recurring theme in Indian policy documents.  In 1849, the government offered private companies a guaranteed 5 per cent annual return on the capital they invested to build the railways, backed by free land and licences running up to 100 years. It was, in effect, an early and appropriate instrument for derisking a market that London investors knew nothing about. The confidence this created was remarkable. British capital flowed into the East Indian Railway (1849), the Great Indian Peninsula Railway (1849), and the Madras Railway (1853). Oversight in this era came from contracts. Each company’s terms were negotiated separately, with the government approving plans and regulating fares. There was no uniform statute governing fares or operations until the Indian Railways Act of 1890. The results were remarkable. From a single 21-mile line in 1853, the network grew to roughly 9,000 miles by 1880. By 1912, the capital invested in the Indian railways stood at roughly ₹477 crore. This amount was cited in a paper titled “The Growth Contribution of Colonial Indian Railways in Comparative Perspective”, co-authored by Dan Bogart, a prominent American economic historian at the University of California, Irvine. The capital of ₹477 crore in 1912, if compounded at 7.4 per cent a year (current 10-year G-Sec rate) over 114 years, would be about ₹16.3 trillion in today’s terms.  If the railways showed what private capital could do on a national scale, tramways showed what could be done at city level. Bombay’s first tram system was private: A company licensed under a Bombay Presidency law in 1874 to ply horse-drawn carriages. When it could not fund electrification, a new private company, the Bombay Electric Supply and Tramways Company (BEST), bought it out in 1905 and electrified the network by 1907. The city took it over only in 1947. Calcutta, Madras and Delhi followed with their own municipally licensed tramways between 1880 and 1908, run by private companies under municipal licences. They were built on an exclusive right to operate rather than a sovereign-backed return, along with a buy-back option that the city could exercise.  Electricity followed a similar city-by-city script. Calcutta Electric Supply Corporation (CESC) lit its first lamps in 1897 under a 21-year licence covering just 5.64 square miles. Tata’s hydroelectric venture, incorporated in 1910, also ran India’s earliest long-distance bulk-power transmission, wheeling power from Khopoli, in the Western Ghats, to Bombay’s textile mills. Ahmedabad followed. The Ahmedabad Electricity Company was floated in 1913 by Bombay-based managing agency Killick, Nixon & Co, with textile baron Ambalal Sarabhai on its board. Then Surat happened in 1920. The Asansol-Raniganj coal belt got its own private power utility in 1919, when Andrew Yule, a British managing agency, set up Dishergarh Power Supply Company to power its collieries. The managing agencies, in short, were, in a way, India’s first private infrastructure entrepreneurs. Not every sector was a success with private capital. In 1853 the government handed its flagship, the Bihar Canal Project, to a private promoter, the East India Irrigation and Canal Company. But by 1868, the government had to buy out the company for ₹10.5 lakh reportedly due to non-performance.  Aviation offers an interesting modern-day parallel. The government built the aerodromes (Calcutta, Allahabad and Bombay in 1924, and Juhu in 1928), while private companies flew the aircraft. Tata launched its Airlines in 1932 out of a palm-thatched hut in Juhu; Govan Bros Ltd floated Indian National Airways in 1933 with ₹3 million of private capital. In 1938 Indian National Airways won a 10-year Empire Air Mail Scheme deal guaranteeing “a minimum income along with an operating subsidy”, a structure strikingly close to the route guarantees used to launch regional air service under India’s UDAN scheme today.  The eventual transition to state ownership, largely completed for the railways by 1944 and for utilities over the following decades, is often told as the end of the story: Private capital’s retreat. However, private capital had done what it was brought in to do: Proving the possibilities of private funding, building and operating assets, and training generations of Indian engineers and managers. Managing agencies like Andrew Yule, Bird & Co, Jardine, and James Finlay too played a pioneering role in building India’s coal, tea, mines and jute economies alongside this infrastructure rollout.  Thus, 150 years ago, private capital proved itself capable of building the rails and power lines of a growing economy. It is a legacy modern India would do well to claim with pride, and to build on with even greater ambition. 
The writer is an infrastructure expert. He is also founder & managing trustee of The Infravision Foundation.With research inputs by Mutum Chaobisana     Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: RBI's forex curbs have steadied the rupee and revived investor sentiment
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / RBI's forex curbs have steadied the rupee and revived investor sentimentRBI's forex curbs have steadied the rupee and revived investor sentiment

It is the stable rupee, not the blue wave in the US

premium

Illustration: Binay Sinha

T T Ram Mohan6 min read Last Updated : Nov 12 2026 | 9:52 PM ISTIndians — and others in the United States (US) and elsewhere — jubilant over the blue wave that swept the Democrats to power in the US Congress, got a cold reality check last week. US President Donald Trump elevated one of his aides, Stephen Miller, as White House chief of staff.  Mr Miller has been characterised as an anti-immigration hawk. He is better characterised as an economic nationalist and a passionate advocate of Mr Trump’s “America First” programme. Absolutely central to that programme is the use of tariffs to advance America’s interests.  Mr Miller is not the principal exponent of tariffs in the Trump administration. Nevertheless, his elevation is important in that it signals that there will be no retreat from Mr Trump’s ideological agenda. That means, among other things, that the world cannot expect the slightest relief with respect to tariffs. India must brace itself for more tough negotiations on the long-pending India-US trade deal. There will be no respite with respect to H-1B visas either.  The seriously good news for India is not the blue wave but the turnaround on the home front of a sort that few had expected. The rupee has appreciated consequent to the forex measures the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) announced last month. In October, it looked as though the rupee would slide below 97 to the dollar in what looked like a free fall. Instead, the rupee has appreciated to above 94.  The RBI’s measures, which curbed the demand for dollars, are not the only reason for the appreciation of the rupee. Global factors have contributed. Investors are retreating from artificial-intelligence (AI) stocks. Yields on US Treasuries have eased. The price of crude oil has dropped to below $100 per barrel.  But the RBI’s measures are undoubtedly an important factor. By containing expectations about rupee depreciation, they appear to have revived foreign institutional investors’ (FIIs’) appetite for Indian stocks. Market pundits who claimed that India had fallen off the radar of foreign investors may well end up looking foolish.  The RBI’s position is that it is not out to defend any particular level of the rupee. Its measures in October were only about preventing “excessive” speculation. “Excessive” speculation is hard to define or determine. The RBI governor said that one-third of all foreign-exchange derivative trades were being cancelled or closed out on the same day they were initiated. He also pointed to one-sided bets against the rupee. It’s not clear why either should be regarded as “excessive”. Both transactions could merely reflect expectations that the rupee is likely to depreciate.  Speculation is unhealthy when it threatens to destabilise the system, say, when large bets are taken with little capital to support them, or when groups of participants are colluding to push the exchange rate in a particular direction. A sudden decline in the exchange rate is also unhealthy when it points to market dysfunction, for example, when small transactions result in large movements in the exchange rate.    There was no evidence of any of these, yet the RBI thought it necessary to intervene in the forex market. It did so for another compelling reason: Too steep a fall in the exchange rate in a short period can be self-reinforcing and result in overshooting. When the rupee depreciates by a large percentage over a certain period, investors such as FIIs become jittery. They see that depreciation is eroding their dollar returns. They head for the exit, which causes the rupee to depreciate even further. By intervening to stabilise the rupee, the RBI can contain a perceived currency risk. That improves the prospects of FIIs entering the market instead of exiting, thereby causing the rupee to appreciate.  That is exactly what seems to have happened after the RBI announced its curbs on dollar demand in October. FII flows were hugely negative in April, May and June in the current financial year. They turned positive in July and August (apparently because of primary-market investment while selling in secondary markets continued). FII flows turned negative again in September and October.  The RBI announced its curbs on the demand for dollars on October 10. By October 16, the rupee had appreciated to 94.96 to the dollar from its level of 96.82 on October 8. At that point, FIIs turned net buyers and they remained net buyers for 14 sessions thereafter up to November 6. In the first six days of November, FII inflows into equities were greater than the outflows in each of the months of September and October.    When the RBI announced its measures, critics said the curbs could not be sustained for long.  When the forex curbs are removed, the rupee will be under pressure if oil prices rise above $100. They are right but it’s also true that sentiment is a big factor in the markets. Intervention of the sort the RBI has undertaken helps turn around sentiment in many ways.  First, speculators betting against the rupee end up suffering losses when curbs on dollar demand cause the rupee to appreciate. Such losses impair their capacity to bet against the rupee once normalcy is restored. Second, the RBI has sent out a signal that one-way bets can be costly. Market participants will think twice before they bet against the rupee after the curbs are removed.  Third, market expectations of a steep depreciation in the rupee become less entrenched. This encourages FIIs to invest in Indian equities. FII inflows, in turn, contribute to further appreciation of the rupee. That is how the vicious spiral of rupee depreciation in the previous months now promises to turn virtuous.  When the RBI announced its forex measures in October, critics refused to buy its position that it was not defending any particular value of the rupee.  They said the RBI was doing precisely that. The talk in the market and in the media was that an exchange rate of ₹97 to the dollar was a line in the sand for the RBI.    Let us say the market thinks the rupee should fall to 100 in three months. The RBI thinks that should happen in one year and intervenes to prevent a sharp fall towards 100. Its intervention results in the rupee stabilising  at 98. Is that a defence of the rupee or preventing unhealthy speculation? Let the pundits and market experts quibble. For now, the success of the RBI’s measures is cause for celebration.

entry.title: India's workplace gender gap persists despite laws and high-profile firsts
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / India's workplace gender gap persists despite laws and high-profile firstsIndia's workplace gender gap persists despite laws and high-profile firsts

Women remain under-represented in Indian corporate leadership and earn less than men, highlighting the gap between workplace policies and actual gender equality.

premium

Gender diversity in corporate India remains a work in progress, with women under-represented in leadership roles and facing a significant pay gap, according to an ILO survey.

Kanika Datta5 min read Last Updated : Nov 11 2026 | 10:03 PM ISTEvery time a woman professional is appointed to a significant role for the first time, the media reports with breathless excitement. The first Indian woman to make partner in a Big Four firm, the first woman to head a bank, the first Indian woman to set up and receive approval for a mutual fund house, the first woman to head a financial watchdog or the competition regulator… all of these are duly hailed as unassailable signs of India’s march toward gender equality in the workplace. No interview of the woman concerned is complete without the obligatory question of “what it feels like to make it in a man’s world” or variations thereof. At the same time, few women in senior roles escape scrutiny on their appearance and attire.   No one has highlighted her irritation with this treatment more forcefully than Nirmala Sitharaman — yes, India’s first woman finance minister and currently the longest-serving one. A rarity in the Indian political firmament as a politician in her own right — not somebody’s wife, sister or mother — she has repeatedly stressed that she does not appreciate media discussions of her sari choices and appearance during the annual Budget presentation, pointing out that such observations put unnecessary stress on women.  Ms Sitharaman may be overstating the case; certainly, in this newspaper, her policies are subject to far more scrutiny than her appearance. But the larger point must be conceded. In the past three-plus decades, as women have begun to play a more conspicuous role in the white-collar executive world and public life in general, the routine practice of gender highlighting and the arch lines of questioning and commentary are revelatory. They actually tell you how little progress white-collar India has made in bridging the gender gap in the workplace.  This was clear from the latest International Labour Organization’s (ILO) survey, which shows that women remain hugely under-represented in Indian corporations and, worse, lag their male peers in earnings. This third edition of the survey, titled “Women in Business and Management: Scaling Success”, covered 11,957 enterprises in 99 countries. India accounted for the highest number of enterprises surveyed, with 768 respondents. Its findings are far from reassuring for a country that sees itself as an emerging global power.  Women accounted for just 12 per cent of managerial positions in India, putting it near the bottom (32nd) among 34 Asia-Pacific economies, ahead of only Pakistan and Bangladesh. Although women at the top are paid on a par with men, most women managers in India earn 28 per cent less than their male counterparts — the fourth-highest gender pay gap in Asia-Pacific. Only Tonga, the Republic of Korea (a surprise) and Vanuatu do worse.  The irony of this data is hard to miss. The past three decades have seen more federal laws and regulations enacted to enable corporations to provide a conducive environment for hiring women. From paid maternity benefits (upgraded in 2017) to paternity leave (1999), compulsory provision of crèches (2017), robust laws mandating protection against sexual harassment in the workplace (2013), and mandatory reservation of board seats for women (2014), India leads several advanced economies in this respect (the US, for instance, does not have a federal law guaranteeing paid maternity leave).  These policies have not resulted in a meaningful change in institutional gender balances because they are either not implemented, applied in such a perfunctory fashion as to make them useless in practice, or not tailored to socio-political realities. Maternity benefits and leave are a case in point. Most companies allow for the legal limit of 26 weeks of paid leave. Some more enlightened companies even allow up to 15 days of paternity leave (though there is no legal mandate for this in the private sector). The ILO survey shows that maternity benefits and support measures are rated the most effective initiatives to retain women. Yet, too many Indian organisations expect new mothers to resume the same level of efficiency and productivity as before. Though this is not an unreasonable expectation from the organisation’s point of view, it ignores the reality that the burden of childcare in India remains woman- and mother-centric, and explains why women leave in droves after they have children. In one of the ILO’s case studies, the Indian arm of the French media and advertising giant Havas introduced a successful “Maternity Bounce Back” initiative that helped new mothers manage their return, including part-time and hybrid work options.  Equally, traditional prejudices about “women’s jobs” constrain the ambit of employment. HR, accounting, and administration are considered posts fit for women to employ; marketing, maybe, but anything approaching consequential decision-making remains a male preserve, despite the presence of the mandatory woman appointee in the boardroom  It is increasingly clear that laws and regulations can only go so far in bridging the gender gap unless male-oriented managements shed their prejudices. Havas, which is headed by a man, has more than doubled the representation of women in its workforce from 19 to 43 per cent over four years by creating a targeted strategy to hire and retain women.  But its chief human resource officer underlined that the effort demands sustained hard work. Few corporations are willing to devote managerial mind-space to an issue seen as peripheral to the bottom line and disruptive of comfortable male-only cultures. So, women’s achievements will continue to be judged as gender-inflected exceptions rather than as part of a gender-neutral norm.   Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer.
